extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of natural philosophy, physicians, and readers interested in scientific method (educated lay readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive method for investigating natural phenomena: begin from clear first principles, deduce ordinary consequences, and then use experiments and observations to resolve particulars; include guidance on exposition, publication, and criteria for attributing mind. Draws on anatomy, mechanics, and thought-experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical certainty rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept as true nothing that did not appear to me more clear and certain than the demonstrations of the geometers had formerly appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard of clarity and certainty exemplified by geometric proofs as the threshold for belief. The author reports this rule enabled him to resolve principal philosophical difficulties quickly; it functions as the initial epistemic filter (anti-pattern: assent to ideas less certain than geometrical demonstrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start from first causes / natural germs
rubrics_metrics.description: Find in general the principles, or first causes of all that is or can be in the world, ... without educing them from any other source than from certain germs of truths naturally existing in our minds (and, in the author's account, taking God as a primary principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground inquiry on fundamental, self-evident principles (innate 'germs' of truth) and use them as premises for deductions. These first causes are the basis for deriving ordinary phenomena; do not rely on ad hoc assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought-experiment isolation (new-world device)
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak only of what would happen in a new world, if God were now to create somewhere in the imaginary spaces matter sufficient to compose one, and were to agitate variously and confusedly the different parts of this matter ... and thereafter do nothing more than lend his ordinary concurrence to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hypothetical 'new world' to isolate variables and avoid entanglement with existing learned disputes. This device permits free theorizing about how simple initial laws and matter must arrange themselves (anti-pattern: carrying over contested scholastic assumptions into fundamental theorizing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select principal aspects for exposition (focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like painters who ... select one of the chief [faces] on which alone they make the light fall, and throwing the rest into the shade ... I resolved to expound singly, though at considerable length, my opinions regarding light; then to take the opportunity of adding something on the sun and the fixed stars ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a subject is complex, focus exposition on the principal aspect to make the account clear and manageable. Cast subsidiary topics into the shade unless needed to illuminate the main point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic forms; use notions natural to the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: I expressly supposed that [matter] possessed none of those forms or qualities which are so debated in the schools, nor in general anything the knowledge of which is not so natural to our minds that no one can so much as imagine himself ignorant of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate hypotheses using concepts directly accessible to ordinary understanding and sensory experience, rather than relying on contested scholastic categories or obscure metaphysical distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive laws necessarily from God's perfection (deductive grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have pointed out what are the laws of nature; and, with no other principle upon which to found my reasonings except the infinite perfection of God, I endeavored to demonstrate all those about which there could be any room for doubt ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek laws that follow necessarily from the chosen foundational principles. Use logical deduction from these principles to show that certain laws must hold (illustration: deduction that certain arrangements of matter will produce heavens, stars, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of inquiry: principles → ordinary effects → particular experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: First, I have essayed to find in general the principles, or first causes ... In the second place, I examined what were the first and most ordinary effects that could be deduced from these causes; ... afterwards when I wished to descend to the more particular ... it is necessary to avail ourselves of many particular experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a staged approach: (1) establish first principles, (2) deduce the common/ordinary consequences, (3) perform targeted experiments to resolve special or detailed phenomena. This sequence reduces confusion and the risk of being misled by rare anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ordinary/common phenomena before rare/recondite
rubrics_metrics.description: At the commencement, it is better to make use only of what is spontaneously presented to our senses, and of which we cannot remain ignorant ... the more uncommon often only mislead us so long as the causes of the more ordinary are still unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin empirical work with common, easily observed phenomena; reserve investigation of rare or special cases until after ordinary causes are well understood. Anti-pattern: privileging obscure phenomena early and drawing broad conclusions from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct observation and dissection for anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: I advise those who are not versed in anatomy, before they commence the perusal of these observations, to take the trouble of getting dissected in their presence the heart of some large animal ... and to have shown to them its two ventricles or cavities ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before theorizing about physiological mechanisms, observe dissected specimens and bodily structures directly. Combine visual inspection with tactile sensations (e.g., feeling heat) to ground hypotheses in observable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic / structural-functional explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion which I have now explained follows as necessarily from the very arrangement of the parts, which may be observed in the heart by the eye alone, and from the heat which may be felt with the fingers, and from the nature of the blood as learned from experience, as does the motion of a clock from the power, the situation, and shape of its counterweights and wheels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain biological and physical phenomena by reference to the arrangement, properties, and mechanical interactions of parts, using analogies to machines where appropriate. Emphasize observable structure and regular mechanical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental demonstration and inference
rubrics_metrics.description: I need only mention in reply what has been written by a physician of England ... by binding the arm with a tie ... cause the blood to flow more copiously ... and ... by cutting a single artery ... all the blood ... may flow out of it in a very short time ... from the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, repeatable experiments (e.g., ligature, incision) to test and support physiological hypotheses. Infer the existence of hidden passages or circuits from experimental outcomes and manipulations (illustration: evidence for circulation from ligature tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain phenomena by observable causes (e.g., heat, rarefaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The blood ... being rarefied, and, as it were, distilled by passing through the heart, it is thinner, and more vivid, and warmer immediately after leaving the heart ... the operation which converts the juice of food into blood ... is distilled by passing and repassing through the heart perhaps more than one or two hundred times in a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for changes in substances and bodily processes by appeal to proximate, observable physical causes (heat, rarefaction, passage through organs) and their effects on material properties (consistency, color, function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate results publicly to promote collective progress
rubrics_metrics.description: I judged that there could be no more effectual provision against these two impediments than if I were faithfully to communicate to the public all the little I might myself have found, and incite men of superior genius to strive to proceed farther, by contributing ... to the experiments which it would be necessary to make, and also by informing the public of all they might discover ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish and share findings so others can perform experiments, build cumulatively, and extend discoveries. The author frames publication as a civic duty to promote the general good and accelerate progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about premature publication and social consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: I learned that persons ... had condemned a certain doctrine ... and this led me to fear lest among my own doctrines likewise some one might be found ... which might tend to the hurt of any one. This has been sufficient to make me alter my purpose of publishing them ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the duty to publish with prudence: avoid publicizing ideas that are insufficiently certain or likely to cause prejudice, social harm, or censorship. Consider religious and political context before dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-utility priority (especially medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: By them I perceived it to be possible to arrive at knowledge highly useful in life; ... especially for the preservation of health, which is ... the first and fundamental [blessing] ... I designed to employ my whole life in the search after so necessary a science ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and prioritize lines of inquiry that promise practical applications—arts, technologies, and medicine. Use theoretical work to guide inventions and remedies that improve human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for attributing reason / rational soul
rubrics_metrics.description: There would still remain two most certain tests whereby to know that [machines] were not therefore really men. Of these the first is that they could never use words or other signs arranged in such a manner as is competent to us ... The second test is, that although such machines might execute many things ... they would, without doubt, fail in certain others from which it could be discovered that they did not act from knowledge, but solely from the disposition of their organs: for while reason is an universal instrument that is alike available on every occasion, these organs, on the contrary, need a particular arrangement for each particular action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether an entity possesses reason or a rational soul, use (1) capacity to produce and use combinatorial language/signs to declare thoughts, and (2) generality of action across novel situations (acting from universal reason rather than fixed organ dispositions). Examples: parrots utter words but do not use language to express thoughts; deaf-mute humans invent signs and thereby demonstrate rationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer deduction from causes over enumerating species/forms
rubrics_metrics.description: It appeared to me impossible for the human mind to distinguish the forms or species of bodies that are upon the earth ... unless we rise to causes through their effects, and avail ourselves of many particular experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than cataloguing surface species or forms, aim to ascend to causes (explain effects by causes) and then use experiments to discriminate particulars. This reduces the burden of endless classification and yields explanatory power.
